EDA’s Future Is Evidence-Driven Automation

Shares

AI may accelerate semiconductor design, but users still need formal proof, semantic continuity, and auditable workflows to trust automation.

September 24th, 2026 -

By: Ann Steffora Mutschler

Key Takeaways:

AI’s biggest EDA opportunity is workflow-level orchestration that coordinates tools, people, constraints, and domain knowledge across traditionally fragmented design stages, rather than merely improving individual tools.
Trust requires evidence and semantic continuity. AI-generated recommendations or assertions must preserve design intent and remain independently verifiable through deterministic verification, formal proof, reproducibility, and audit trails.
The emerging EDA model is human-guided, agentic automation. AI handles repetitive coordination, exploration, debugging, and handoffs, while engineers retain control over specifications and signoff. Established EDA engines provide the ground truth.

AI is arriving in EDA at a time when engineers can no longer depend on brute-force scaling for performance and power improvements, and when the gaps created by disconnected point tools are becoming increasingly time-consuming to fill.
As designs expand to tens of billions of transistors and incorporate chiplets in multi-die assemblies, the hardest problems increasingly sit between tools — preserving intent, managing interdependencies, and identifying potential failures before they reach tapeout. At advanced nodes, where design costs can reach hundreds of millions of dollars and a single respin can threaten an entire program, AI’s real value will depend on whether it can accelerate various steps in the design flow while organizing and interpreting the data needed to trust the results.
The balance is between reliability and practicality. The global shortage of skilled engineers has not gone away. But it has made workflow automation more attractive, provided it can either improve the productivity of human engineers or achieve comparable results.
“Every customer is saying, ‘Give me the ability to shrink my time to results by at least 2×,’” said Ankur Gupta, executive vice president and head of EDA IC software at Siemens EDA. “Demand is pushing EDA toward a new operating model built on faster engines, smarter execution, and trusted outcomes. Acceleration may come from GPUs, machine learning, or reinforcement learning, but the larger goal is to shorten design cycles without losing confidence in the result.”
Efficiency also matters at the agent layer. Allowing any agent to call any tool may be flexible, but it can be expensive and inefficient if the underlying interfaces are poorly written. The goal is to do more of that integration work in advance so customers can either use a vendor’s agents or their own without paying unnecessary token and orchestration costs.
The economics of AI are becoming increasingly important as engineers incorporate it at various places in the design process.
“If I spend more money on tokens than a human would cost, then it doesn’t make sense,” said Thomas Andersen, vice president of the AI Excellence Group at Synopsys. “Agentic AI is useful only when it reduces the cost and complexity of production workflows. An agentic loop can perform sequences of tasks that an expert would otherwise handle manually, from automating repetitive steps to coordinating work across tools. Everybody wants to automate their workflows. They want agentic automation because that’s their way to productivity, to faster tape-out cycles, cutting costs, everything.”
The hard part isn’t dropping a tool. It’s integrating agents into real customers’ design flows.
Current challenges
Semiconductor design is inherently a multi-tool process, spanning architecture, IP configuration, integration, verification, implementation, and sign-off. The challenge is not simply moving data from one tool to another, but preserving the design intent, assumptions, and engineering context behind that data. “At the system level, where connectivity, address maps, performance constraints, and security requirements must remain consistent across many IP blocks and, increasingly, across multiple dies, engineers often serve as the integration layer,” explained Andy Nightingale, vice president of product management and marketing at Arteris.
That becomes increasingly difficult as systems grow in complexity. “The same architectural intent may be represented differently across integration, performance analysis, verification, and implementation environments,” Nightingale said. “If those representations diverge, the result can be additional verification cycles, manual rework, and late discovery of system-level issues. Better optimization between tools therefore needs to provide semantic continuity across the design flow, not simply file-format interoperability.”
Still, AI’s real impact on EDA will be less about sign-off and more about streamlining the peripheral process and data-management work around the flow. “There’s as much value there now as in the core simulators and layout tools, and that’s where AI can help you get things done much faster,” said Chris Mueth, new opportunities business manager at Keysight EDA.
Chip design is essentially a relay race involving dozens of specialized tools, including architectural exploration, RTL, lint, clock-domain crossing, formal, simulation, synthesis, place-and-route, timing and power sign-off, physical verification, equivalence checking, DFT, and post-silicon correlation.
“Each was written by a different vendor, against a different data model, with different assumptions about what ‘done’ means,” said Ashish Darbari, CEO of Axiomise. “The relay is where most of the pain lives. As the Agentic Electronic Design Automation: A Handoff Perspective survey puts it, EDA is ‘inherently multi-stage and handoff-heavy,’ and every artifact crosses tool, session, and organizational boundaries before signoff. Each transfer is a chance to lose information, silently reinterpret intent, or push a decision that was locally optimal in one tool into a globally suboptimal position downstream.”
Darbari groups the core workflow challenges into a few recurring failure modes:

No shared semantic model. Synthesis, P&R, and signoff are still optimized for local objectives because they cannot reliably see downstream consequences. Integrated platforms help within one vendor stack, but semantic gaps remain wide across vendors and between design and verification.
Handoff loss between design and verification. RTL often carries intent that never makes it into machine-checkable form, forcing engineers to re-derive testbenches, assertions, coverage models, constraints, and waivers from ambiguous English. Silicon success data underscores the cost. First-time silicon success has fallen sharply, with most respins still traced to design errors. That is a workflow and intent-transfer problem, not simply a compute problem.
Fragmented data formats and closed databases. A common, vendor-neutral data model is still missing, so cross-tool AI efforts often begin by rebuilding parsers instead of applying intelligence to the design problem.
The reconciliation tax. Engineers spend significant time reconciling constraints, waivers, timing exceptions, coverage exclusions, and floorplan intent between adjacent tools. Much of that work is bookkeeping to keep the flow coherent, not verification itself.
Local optima, global pain. A tool can meet its local target while creating downstream closure problems, such as a congestion-hostile netlist or a hold issue that triggers another ECO loop. The opportunity is to optimize across boundaries, not just within them.
Trustworthy EDA. Tools also have bugs, including signoff tools. Pardalos, Donaldson, Morini, Pozzi, and Wickerson’s Who checks the checkers? paper showed that Equifuzz uncovered 16 distinct bugs across three major commercial C-to-RTL equivalence checkers, including unsoundness cases where non-equivalent designs were declared equivalent. The lesson reaches beyond equivalence checking: AI can automate handoffs only if it preserves not just data, but the assumptions, limits, and evidential status of each result.

That is why the next phase of AI in EDA is shifting from optimizing individual tools to coordinating the people, engines, and domain knowledge that sit between them.
Solaiman Rahim, chief product officer at ChipAgents, said tool-level AI has already improved individual engines, but the larger opportunity is coordinating the dependencies between tools and people. A DFT engineer, for example, may complete insertion correctly but still need timing analysis, expert interpretation, and another round of fixes before the work is usable. Each handoff can add days. “If you have a DFT agent handling DFT insertion and a timing agent that runs timing and debugs timing, these two agents can work together to speed up the process,” Rahim said. “Instead of taking weeks, it can take potentially just hours.”
That speedup requires more than scripts. Workflows need access to methodology, design knowledge, and context accumulated across teams. Rahim described an ontology layer that can capture why expert engineers avoid certain cells, choose particular constraints, or debug recurring failures, then make that know-how available to less experienced users and to coordinated AI workflows.
The same need for workflow-level coordination shows up outside the core digital flow, particularly where physical analysis depends on moving design data, assumptions, and results across multiple engineering domains. Satish Radhakrishnan, head of go-to-market for semiconductor and electronics at Vinci, said physics-based analysis faces the same workflow problem. Specialized tools may work well on their own, but model preparation, data movement, specialist handoffs, and result interpretation still slow the loop. By the time the analysis returns, the design may already have changed.
The problem grows as chips, packages, and systems become more tightly coupled. A chip-level change can affect package and board temperatures, mechanical stress, warpage, and reliability, none of which respects the boundary between tools or teams.
Radhakrishnan said much of the delay occurs before a solver starts. Engineers still clean geometry, create meshes, apply materials and boundary conditions, and hand results between design and simulation specialists. That process may support scheduled analysis, but it cannot provide reliable feedback each time a design changes. The goal, he said, is to move from isolated simulation checkpoints to continuous physics reasoning inside the design workflow.
Where EDA workflows are headed
ChipAgent’s Rahim predicts that the next layer of AI assistance will depend on understanding design intent, not just parsing cells and wires. “In SoC debug, for example, an AI system that understands the instruction being executed, the memory operation involved, and the relevant cycles in a waveform can help narrow a failure the way an expert designer would. The value comes from pairing intent recognition with an intelligence layer that can take action across the workflow.”
As part of this, requirements management is essential. “Today’s AI still has room for error, so you don’t let it own specifications or sign-off,” said Keysight’s Meuth. “You use it to accelerate the workflow around those decisions, not to make the decisions themselves.”
These safeguards are being implemented wherever AI is used. Paul Graykowski, director of product marketing at Cadence, pointed to one guardrail for AI-assisted testbench enhancement. Rather than allowing an agent to rewrite code unilaterally, the system surfaces the proposed refactoring for review. “The tool actually picks up those differences, and it will propose fixes,” Graykowski said. “It’s going to look at it and just say, ‘Okay, here’s the refactoring I’m proposing. Take a look at it. Do you approve?'”
That same approval model can support more autonomous regression repair, as long as the changes remain isolated until an engineer accepts them. Graykowski said one customer wanted an agent to analyze failures, make candidate fixes, rerun the regression, and return with a sandboxed result: “I’ve created a snapshot of your code, I’ve gone off, and I’ve worked on it in this sandbox. Here are the changes I’ve made. Do you approve these changes now?”
Darbari sees three emerging ways AI can reduce cross-tool friction, ranging from near-term optimization to deeper infrastructure changes. But he draws a sharp distinction between automation that preserves context and automation that simply adds another agent to the relay.

Cross-boundary optimization loops. This is the most mature AI use case in EDA — learning which settings, constraints, and tool sequences work together across comparable designs. The value is not that AI writes better code, but that it can reduce the reconciliation tax by learning and reusing combinations that improve productivity, compute efficiency, and PPA from RTL to GDSII.
Agentic pipelines and copilot layers. Tools such as Synopsys.ai Copilot, Cadence ChipStack and AuraStack, and Siemens Fuse point toward a workflow layer that can connect architecture, RTL, verification, and physical design. But that layer needs safeguards. LLMs do not inherently understand native EDA data, design intent, production-security requirements, or the limits of their own outputs.
AI as an interoperability layer. If the second layer orchestrates tools, the third gives agents a shared representation of what those tools produce. Vendor-neutral efforts such as Si2’s Schema Ontology and Accellera’s CDC/RDC Integration Standard point to abstractions that let agents reason across tools without rebuilding context at every step. Without that common substrate, AI may accelerate tool use but still lose meaning at the boundaries.

For formal verification, AI is most valuable when handoff loss is high. “LLMs can extract properties, suggest assertions, propose abstractions, and triage proofs. However, AI outputs must be independently verified, as generated assertions are hypotheses, not proof. Only a completed proof against a correct property counts as evidence. A prompt is not proof,” Darbari said.
Cadence’s Graykowski noted that kind of checked assistance could also lower the barrier to formal verification for teams without deep formal expertise. If engineers can define intent or provide a specification, an agent can help generate candidate properties and check code before it reaches simulation or a formal engine such as Jasper. The point is not to replace formal expertise, but to move more designs toward machine-checkable evidence earlier in the flow.
Further, Darbari observed that single-tool AI features are becoming table stakes. “The next competitive frontier is between tools — agentic orchestration, standardized data models, and the ability to move constraints, waivers, and evidence across tool boundaries without loss. The FluxBench evaluation of AI agents attempting end-to-end RTL-to-GDSII is a sobering reminder that the seams are still hard. The problem is not the AI. It is the lack of a shared semantic substrate for the AI to reason over.”
The need for a shared semantic substrate is where orchestration becomes more than automation. The agent has to understand not only which tool to call next, but what each result means in the larger system context.
AI can provide an intelligent orchestration layer across EDA tools. “Rather than requiring an engineer to manually inspect every result and determine the next action, an AI agent can correlate information from multiple tools, understand the wider system context, and recommend or execute the appropriate next step,” Arteris’ Nightingale said. “For example, it could identify a system-level performance issue, relate that issue to an architectural or configuration decision, make a controlled change, and rerun the relevant analysis to determine whether the result has improved.”
A fundamental shift in AI’s evolution involves moving from operating inside individual tools to operating between tools. Standardized interfaces can make EDA capabilities accessible to agents, but tool access alone is not enough.
“AI also needs domain-specific context, a consistent representation of design intent, controlled permissions, and measurable results against which its actions can be checked. In this model, AI provides reasoning and orchestration while established EDA engines continue to provide deterministic analysis and verification,” Nightingale explained.
Rahim expects compute to keep moving up the stack, first from tools to workflows, and eventually from workflows into chip-design-specific models. Today’s frontier models are not yet specialized, cost-effective, or physically aware enough to generate fully verified, PPA-optimized RTL, analog layouts, advanced packaging, or netlists on demand. But he believes that capability will improve as models absorb more workflow knowledge and domain context. “We are confident we can tackle the problem because our customers are pulling us. Semiconductors are becoming a commodity. The number of projects they have to do, the number of layouts, and the analog experts they have available no longer scale. Because of that, our customers need a solution in that space, and they are looking for a partner to work with. They are willing to share a lot of that layout knowledge for us to train on.”
Additionally, Vinci’s Radhakrishnan said that AI can remove repetitive work around physics analysis by preparing inputs, invoking the right tools, carrying results forward, and comparing alternatives within engineer-defined boundaries. But the agent is only as useful as the analysis beneath it. If simulation still requires hours of manual setup and days to run, an AI front end does not solve the bottleneck. Agentic workflows become useful when the underlying analysis is fast, automated, deterministic, and production-scale.
In Vinci’s case, the approach is to ingest native design files and pair pretrained physics models with GPU-native numerical physics kernels, producing solver-accurate results without human meshing or customer-specific training data. Radhakrishnan said the point is not probabilistic simulation-by-chatbot, but repeatable physics results that can be used while the design is still changing.

Many companies are now using agentic AI or other types of AI to enhance workflows or optimize tools in the EDA process, as well as for other reasons. Mo Faisal, founder and CEO of Movellus, sees this as an advantage for new companies. “They’re starting from scratch, and I’m a little jealous of companies born in the last month. They don’t have the baggage, at least in Silicon Valley. The most common use I’ve seen is automatic customer ticket triage, customer success, and customer support. You put in the documentation and all of your context. When a customer ticket comes in, it is automatically processed, though there’s still a human in the loop. That workflow is probably the earliest in terms of benefiting from agentic AI first.”

From a product development point of view, agentic AI is being used to create product definition specs and do quick prototyping. “Product management is blurring with engineering,” Faisal observed. “Design is product management and engineering, so the workflow changes are happening there for the open-minded teams,” Faisal noted. “In other areas like legal and accounting, etc., that’s low-hanging fruit, but bringing agentic AI into complex engineering workflow- that’s the really interesting part here. It’s definitely happening. People have libraries of skill files now, so with whatever they’re doing for their workflow, they have a bunch of skill files that are skilled in a certain step; then models are called in as they’re processing that. Yet, while this is true in Silicon Valley, if you go somewhere else, it’s not happening yet.”

Raising the abstraction
As the industry gains experience with AI, EDA workflows are likely to become increasingly intent-driven. “Rather than directly operating every tool and manually translating information between different environments, engineers will increasingly be able to specify objectives such as performance targets, connectivity requirements, security policies, or implementation constraints,” Nightingale said. “AI agents can then help determine which analyses and tools are required to meet those objectives and coordinate the necessary iterations across the design flow.”
This will make verification even more important. As agents are trusted to make larger changes and run longer workflows, every action will need an observable, verifiable outcome. “The most effective future EDA environments are therefore likely to combine AI-driven exploration and orchestration with deterministic engineering tools that continuously provide ground truth. The objective is not autonomous chip design for its own sake, but to reduce repetitive tool interactions and manual translation so engineers can spend more time making architectural and system-level decisions,” he said.
Radhakrishnan said the first challenge is to remove discrete bottlenecks, such as model preparation, analysis setup, and result comparison. Over time, those steps can become part of connected design loops in which an agent proposes a change, initiates the right physics analysis, checks the result against requirements, and either explores another option or sends the design to an engineer for review.
That would enable engineering teams to consider many more ideas. In fact, engineers who now test a handful of options may be able to examine hundreds or thousands, turning design exploration from a scheduled event into an iterative, more creative part of daily engineering work. But Radhakrishnan noted that the boundary between automation and human judgment will still matter. Early exploration may tolerate more autonomy, but validation and signoff require traceability, reproducibility, and deterministic results.
The longer-term opportunity is a design environment where AI agents coordinate specialized tools while deterministic physics keeps pace with the ideas engineers generate. In that model, physical behavior is evaluated throughout the flow, not only at scheduled checkpoints.
Axiomise’s Darbari pointed to visible shifts, each of which he expects to accelerate over the next two to three years. “The first shift is from tool-level AI to flow-level evidence. The first generation of AI in EDA sold productivity. The second will be judged on evidence. A signoff report that says, ‘The AI copilot converged the design in 40% less time,’ is interesting to a project manager. A signoff report that says ‘these properties are proven, these are bounded, these are AI-suggested and not yet checked, here is the reproducibility record,’ is what a safety, security, or automotive customer will accept. The current infatuation with autonomy will give way to an insistence on auditability. The second shift is occurring from simulation confidence to proof-backed signoff. The shift I care about most is from ‘we ran a lot of simulation, and everything looked green’ to ‘we can point at machine-checkable evidence for the properties that matter, and AI helped us get there faster.’ AI-assisted property extraction, agentic coverage closure, and LLM-driven abstraction discovery are real accelerators, but their output has to land on a formal engine that produces deterministic proof, or the confidence is theater. Apple’s Hilbert system, which wraps informal LLM reasoning around Lean 4, is the clearest public example of the architecture that will win. AI for exploration. Formal for correctness closure.”
Another wrinkle is that AI silicon splits into two verification and signoff regimes. “Training hardware lives or dies on distributed progress, collective operations, numerically valid reductions, and silent-data-corruption resilience across large clusters,” Darbari added. “Inference hardware, especially decode-heavy serving, lives on KV-cache ownership, scheduling, isolation, fairness, and tail latency. The cross-tool optimizations that matter for a training accelerator don’t matter for an inference tile. The AI-in-EDA story will fragment along the same lines. AI will not remove the need for handoffs. A boundary will always exist between architectural intent and implementation, between design and verification, and between pre-silicon proof and post-silicon behavior. AI can compress the reconciliation tax at each boundary and give engineers more time for the questions only humans can answer. Use AI for speed. Use formal for truth. Treat the boundaries between tools as places to accumulate evidence, not places to lose it.”
That shift from tool-level automation to flow-level evidence also changes what EDA companies and engineering teams have to organize around.
Organizational changes required
Tool vendors face the same organizational challenge as their customers. Agents built inside individual product groups can recreate the silos they are supposed to remove. Synopsys’ Andersen said the shift has to be guided from the top, not left entirely to bottom-up experimentation. “Every product team tends to say, ‘I’m going to build an agent in my domain, but we have to look at the whole flow.”
That matters because agentic EDA will fail if it simply adds another layer of locally optimized automation. To reduce handoff loss, organizations need shared ownership of the end-to-end flow, common data and permission models, and metrics that measure whether agents improve engineering outcomes rather than merely execute more steps.
Rahim expects workflows to advance over the next six months, especially in root-cause analysis, verification, timing closure, physical design, analog, and advanced packaging. But he cautioned that complex, fully optimized designs remain beyond current frontier models. The likely path, he said, is gradual, with specialized workflows becoming more capable, workflow knowledge moving into model layers, and chip-design models becoming more physically aware through collaboration with customers and foundries.
Graykowski succinctly framed where AI belongs in this flow: “We’re leveraging these tools as assistants, not replacements. You have to guide it. They’re the junior engineer. You’re the senior engineer.”
That may be the most practical way to think about AI’s role in EDA. It will not eliminate the boundaries between specification, implementation, verification, signoff, packaging, and post-silicon learning. Nor will it make probabilistic answers acceptable where deterministic proof is required. Its value will come from what happens at those boundaries: whether agents can carry intent, assumptions, constraints, results, and proof across the flow without losing meaning. If they can, evidence-driven automation becomes more than a productivity story. It becomes the foundation for EDA workflows that execute faster, are easier to audit, and are safer to trust.
